not_modelled.what: 50% subtraction of Connecticut Teachers' Retirement System pay, at any income, as an alternative to the Line 48b subtraction. The projection cannot tell a teachers' pension from another public pension.

Property tax credit: up to 300 a return for property tax paid on a Connecticut home or car, reduced in steps above 49,500 of Connecticut AGI (single; 70,500 MFJ/QSS, 35,250 MFS, 54,500 HOH) and gone above 109,500 (130,500, 65,250, 114,500). The projection does not know the property tax paid.
Interest on U.S. government obligations and the U.S.-obligation share of qualifying mutual fund dividends are subtracted.
Connecticut earned income tax credit: 40% of the federal earned income credit, plus 250 with a qualifying child.
Subtractions for CHET and ABLE account contributions, up to 5,000 (10,000 joint) each.

approximations.what: Tables C (2% phase-out add-back) and D (tax recapture) are step tables of dollar amounts by Connecticut AGI band; the format's recapture fields hold only where each starts, so the amounts are not computed from this file. The full tables are in the record's recapture[].as_printed; a consumer that applies them from there is exact.
approximations.size: The table amount, added to tax: Table C up to 250 (single, MFS), 500 (MFJ/QSS), 400 (HOH); Table D up to 3,400 (single, MFS), 6,800 (MFJ/QSS), 5,320 (HOH). Example: single, Connecticut AGI 300,000: 250 + 2,050 = 2,300 a year too little.

approximations.what: The 50% subtraction for Connecticut teachers' pensions is not applied (not_modelled); above the Line 48b phase-out a retired teacher's pension is taxed in full.
approximations.size: Half the teachers' pension at the marginal rate, for a household with one; nothing otherwise. Example (Aubrey, PDF page 10 Example 2): single, 40,000 of teachers' pay, federal AGI 110,000: the projection subtracts nothing (Connecticut AGI 110,000, tax 5,350.00) where the booklet subtracts 20,000 (90,000, tax 4,200.00): 1,150 a year too much, before Tables C and D.

approximations.what: Roth conversions are not in covers: the booklet does not say whether they qualify for the Line 48b subtraction (covers_unclear in the record). If they do, this overstates tax in a conversion year below the phase-out end.
approximations.size: Up to the marginal rate times 75% of the conversion, only while federal AGI is under 100,000 (single, MFS, HOH) or 150,000 (MFJ); a large conversion usually pushes AGI past that. Example: single, 50,000 of wages and a 20,000 conversion (federal AGI 70,000): if conversions qualify, 15,000 is subtracted (Connecticut AGI 55,000, tax 2,047.50 after the .10 Table E credit) instead of none (70,000, tax 3,100.00): 1,052.50 a year too much.

approximations.what: Interest on U.S. Treasury obligations is taxed (the projection cannot tell it from other interest).
approximations.size: The marginal rate times the Treasury interest. Example: single, Connecticut AGI 60,000 including 10,000 of Treasury interest: tax 2,295.00 instead of 1,800.00 on 50,000 (both after the .10 Table E credit): 495 a year too much.

approximations.what: The property tax credit is not applied (not_modelled).
approximations.size: Up to 300 a year, for a household paying Connecticut property tax with Connecticut AGI under 109,500 (single), 130,500 (MFJ/QSS), 65,250 (MFS) or 114,500 (HOH).

approximations.what: The Pension and Annuity Phase-Out Table names only married filing jointly for its higher column; for a qualifying surviving spouse the booklet does not say which column applies, and the projection's income test has no qualifying_surviving_spouse threshold.
approximations.size: Only a qualifying surviving spouse with federal AGI between 75,000 and 150,000 and pension or IRA income. Example: federal AGI 90,000 with 40,000 of pension: the married filing jointly column subtracts all 40,000 (Connecticut AGI 50,000, tax 646.00); the single column keeps .05 and subtracts 2,000 (88,000, tax 3,114.00): 2,468 a year apart.

approximations.what: Partial Social Security subtraction, married filing separately: the filer is taken to have lived with the spouse at some time in the year, so Line B is the federal worksheet's Line 7 (no base amount), as a projection of one household implies. A separate filer who lived apart all year uses Line 9, after the 25,000 base.
approximations.size: For a separate filer who lived apart all year: 25% of up to 25,000 more stays taxable, up to 6,250, about 437 a year at 6.99%.
